newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Southeast power steady on tight transmission.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Southeast power steady on tight transmission.

text.p: Spot physical electricity prices in the southeastern U.S. finished Thursday steady to higher from Wednesday's level amid transmission contraints within the region, industry sources said.
Sufficent generation capacity combined with mild weather offset upward price pressure from transmission tightness in the Southeastern Electric Reliability Council (SERC) district, traders said.
The threat of Hurricane Lili hitting Florida faded today Lili has become a "non-factor," a Houston trader said. "The Florida utilities are not worried about it at all."
The latest forecasts showed the storm system was moving closer to Cuba and pound the island with heavy winds and torrential rains.

Meanwhile, Georgia Power Co's 1,162 megawatt (MW) Vogtle 2 nuclear power unit in Waynesboro, Ga., was approaching full power following repairs to a malfunctioning feedwater regulator valve late Monday.
At the Georgia/Florida border, next-day firm, peak electricity was unchanged from Wednesday's at $23.00-$24.00 a megawatt hour, with deals heard done today in $22.50-$30.25 range.
Next-day, firm electricity prices during light load hours at the Ga./Fla. border were valued at $13.50-$14.00, a tighter range than Wednesday's $13.00-$14.00.

Up at the northern part of Tennessee Valley Authority's (TVA) distribution sytem, next-day electricity prices for firm, peak delivery were quoted at $17.00-$18.00, up from a quote of $16.00-$17.00 on Wednesday.
Off-peak, firm power in northern TVA for Friday delivery was notationally assessed near $12.00.
TVA reportedly was offering peak, non-firm power for next-day delivery at $20.50, up from Wednesday's $19.50-$20.00.
